B: Hello there! Rutendo, is it? I hope I've said that right. Martin.
A: You said it perfectly, thank you. Hello, Martin.
B: Now, I've heard all about you. Lisa said you make your own dresses and you were dead helpful about her mum.
A: Oh, that's kind of her. And Lisa told me you're a pub quiz man.
B: Geography and sport. Lost by one point again last week. I'm still sore about it.
A: One point, that's painful, yeah.
B: Painful! So where are you, then?
A: Coventry. Twenty years now. I'm originally from Zimbabwe, from Bulawayo.
B: Bulawayo, now I know that from teaching. Matobo Hills, the granite. Balancing rocks. The kids always loved those pictures, they couldn't believe the rocks didn't fall over.
A: Oh, you know the Matobo! Not many people here do. My dad used to take us there when we were small.
B: Is he still out there?
A: He passed away a few years ago. Erm, it's okay. My mum's in Leicester now, with my brother.
B: Sorry, love. Same with mine, my dad. You never quite stop thinking about it, do you.
A: No. You don't. What about you, are you still teaching?
B: No, I finished a couple of years back. Bit of a, er, it got on top of me, all the inspections. I do a bit of invigilating now. And I keep saying I'll volunteer as a guide somewhere. Local history's my thing, the Somerset Levels, the Monmouth Rebellion, battle of Sedgemoor, all that. I've not filled the form in, mind.
A: Oh, you should. I listen to a lot of history podcasts, and the ones I love are always the people who just really care about one little place. You'd be brilliant at that, you know?
B: Well, I'd talk their ears off, that's for sure.
A: That's what a guide is, though. Talking their ears off, but nicely.
B: Ha! Karen'd say there's no nicely about it. What do you do, then?
A: Occupational therapist. Home visits for the council. I spend all day in people's kitchens.
B: Oh, you'd have a field day in ours. Tartan throw, dog hair, the lot.
A: Ha, I like lived-in. Lived-in is what I'm looking for, actually, I want to see how someone really uses their house.
B: And Lisa said you sing as well?
A: Church choir, alto. We're doing something very tricky for Easter.
B: I'm a folk man. Pub sing-arounds. Loud, not always in tune.
A: Loud is half of it! Our choir director would love you, we've got too many quiet people.
B: No, see, I'd be the opposite problem, she'd be telling me to
A: To sing quieter, yes, probably
